title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
description: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.Following
body: Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison."I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing. These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail. Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

schema.headline: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case

title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
description: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him."I want
body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him."I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me." The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.Peña rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation came as Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.Photos taken near Paraguay's Congress building on Thursday show police officers clashing with protesters demanding Peña be removed from office.Paraguay's congress must approve the resignation of a president. But a special session convened on Thursday to address his resignation was adjourned in favour of continuing with the impeachment process.Congress has scheduled a special session for Friday, when Peña is expected to present his defence, according to Reuters news agency. In a post on X, Peña confirmed he would appear for Senate impeachment proceedings, adding that he would do so to "exercise my right to a defence".He wrote: "I will provide the information requested of me. Citizens deserve to know the truth, without cover-ups and without anyone being above the law."Peña earlier said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts. The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.

schema.headline: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse

title: Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayor over incumbent Karen Bass
description: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.Raman's win stunned political watchers in Cali
body: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office. Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms. Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken." "Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us." Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watchFood, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeatRaman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again". She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city. The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster. The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

schema.headline: Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayor over incumbent Karen Bass

title: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension
description: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff betw
body: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule. But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary. But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach. The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency."Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.Mohamud has called for national talks from 14 to 18 November to resolve the deadlock, but opposition leaders have questioned his legitimacy to convene the discussions.The political turmoil comes as Somalia continues to battle al-Shabab, which controls large parts of the countryside despite years of military operations.Uganda, the largest contributor of troops to the African Union mission fighting the militants, announced this week that it planned to withdraw its forces by the end of the year, adding to concerns about Somalia's security.

schema.headline: Somalia's Supreme court rejects President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term extension

title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
description: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to sto
body: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

schema.headline: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck

title: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason
description: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raise
body: Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement."By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement."The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court. He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.But if the four-year sentence is upheld, it would rule him out of the next elections, due in 2030.Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty. Human rights group Amnesty International described his conviction as a "travesty of justice"."Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted," said its regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah:President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.During his time in remand custody at Dar es Salaam's Ukonga Prison, Lissu went on hunger strike twice for brief periods when he said he was not allowed access to his lawyers or relatives. He also complained that guards listened to what should have been private consultations his lawyers.These allegations have been denied by the prison authorities.His case has attracted international attention, with rights groups expressing concern about the treatment of opposition politicians and the shrinking space for political dissent in Tanzania.Last year's election was followed by widespread protests and a violent security crackdown that left at least 500 people dead, according to an official inquiry.Opposition groups have said the death toll was much higher and demanded an independent investigation.The government has defended its handling of the unrest and rejected accusations of widespread political repression.Samia, 66, has insisted the election was fair and transparent and blamed foreigners for the unrest, saying it was part of a plot to overthrow her. She has set up another commission to inquiry to identify those behind the violence.Lissu has long been one of Tanzania's most outspoken critics of the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) party, which, along with its predecessor Tanu, has dominated the country's politics since independence.He first became an MP in 2010, representing a constituency near his birth place in Singida, 320km (200 miles) north-west of the capital, Dodoma.In September 2017, the Chadema politician narrowly survived an assassination attempt when gunmen sprayed his vehicle with bullets outside his home in Dodoma.He was shot multiple times and underwent extensive medical treatment abroad.The attack, whose perpetrators have never been brought to justice, forced him to spend years in exile.He returned to contest the 2020 presidential election against the late President John Magufuli, but lost in a vote that the opposition alleged was marred by widespread irregularities.Lissu subsequently returned to exile before coming back to Tanzania in 2023, following President Samia's decision to lift a ban on opposition political rallies.His return was initially seen as a sign of renewed political openness after years of restrictions under Magufuli, who died in office in 2021.But relations between the government and the opposition deteriorated as the country approached the 2025 election.Lissu became Chadema's national chairman in January 2025 and intensified his demands for electoral reforms.His conviction is likely to deepen concerns about the state of democracy in Tanzania.Last week, Amnesty accused the government of continuing its crackdown following the election and "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear".The authorities did not respond to a request for comment.Correction: An initial version of this story said Lissu had been convicted of inciting treason. We have corrected this to incitement.

schema.headline: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason

title: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in JanuaryByNardine SaadReporting fromLos Angele
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, California Governor Gavin Newsom's term in office comes to an end in JanuaryByNardine SaadReporting fromLos Angeles and Madeline HalpertCalifornia Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison. "We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday. Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.Figure caption, Americans' views on death penalty after failed execution in TennesseeDescribing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me"."As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote. "For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US. He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that"."I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, San Quentin State Prison's used to house California's death row adjustment centreNewsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence. Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions."At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said. Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action."These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said."By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty. "Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.Figure caption, How widely used is the death penalty in the US?On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty. No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley. But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.

schema.headline: California Governor Gavin Newsom commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates

title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
description: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon a
body: A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, about 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries". The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police. French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests indicated there were no traces of alcohol or drugs in his blood. Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock."The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties". Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the accident was tragic, and thanked the firefighters, medical teams and police who attended the scene. Earlier, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

schema.headline: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say

title: Pollution: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared?
description: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air pu
body: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers."The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management. Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.Experts say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement."There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.Others argue that the problem goes much deeper."If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air."We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution."Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains. This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.'I panic every time she coughs' - Delhi's toxic air is making its children sickWhy India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxicCan artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and againIn the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season. Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life. Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants. The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi."I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says."What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

schema.headline: Pollution: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared?

title: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Ova
body: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument."We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.The order does not prevent future presidents from changing the decor of the famous room.The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom. How Trump is remaking the White House in his own imageSigning the new executive order on Thursday, the president said: "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country." He added that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone. Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".

schema.headline: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument

title: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks
description: Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and c
body: Millions across India are set to celebrate Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, illuminating homes, temples, offices and streets with oil lamps and colourful lights to symbolise the triumph of light over darkness.The festival falls on the darkest night of the Hindu lunar month of Kartik, when the moon is not visible in the sky.Although Diwali traditions vary across India's regions and communities, the festival is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, the exchange of sweets and the lighting of firecrackers.But the celebrations come amid growing concerns over air pollution, particularly in northern India.Seasonal weather conditions and the burning of crop residue contribute to deteriorating air quality, while firecrackers set off during Diwali can make the situation worse.In the capital, Delhi, the air quality index (AQI) reached 391 on Friday morning, placing it in the "very poor" category ahead of the festival. There are fears that pollution levels could rise further after the celebrations.India's financial capital, Mumbai, has also experienced high pollution levels in recent weeks, with its AQI reaching 322 on 24 October. Although air quality has improved in recent days to reach "moderate" levels of 104 on Friday, there are concerns that Diwali fireworks could trigger another spike.In an effort to limit pollution, India's Supreme Court on Monday permitted the manufacture, sale and use of certified "green" firecrackers in Delhi and surrounding areas for a limited period.These firecrackers are designed to produce 20-30% less emissions than conventional fireworks. But critics have questioned how effective they are in reducing pollution and raised concerns that conventional firecrackers could still make their way into the capital from neighbouring states.

schema.headline: Diwali 2026: Indians celebrate festival with lights and fireworks

title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
description: Figure caption, Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answersByNick BeakeEurope correspondentRelatives of Britons killed in this summer
body: Figure caption, Families of Britons killed in Spain wildfires demand answersByNick BeakeEurope correspondentRelatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in."If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.He lost his father Michael and his dad's partner Christine.The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe."It's just outrageous. It's an injustice. As family members, we're absolutely disgusted. This is an insult," says Duncan Chard.The families also say their grief has been made worse by how police have handled their loved ones' remains and belongings since the fire.'Issue the damned alert!'Michael Chard built his house in Bédar from scratch. "He called it Casa Micas," his son said. "It was his place in the sun, it was his little paradise."On the morning of the fire, Michael's partner Christine had met friends and was due to go to the hairdresser. "Then everything changed... the whole world changed for them," he said.Image source, Courtesy of the Chard familyImage caption, Christine and Michael Chard are among the 15 people killed in July's deadly wildfire in the village of BédarDuncan Chard said his father, who had two artificial knees and walked with a stick, left his house with Christine as soon as they saw the flames. They left their phones and passports behind and tried to escape by car, but the road was blocked."This is an action of a brave person who was fighting to the end," he said.Andalusia's emergencies chief, Antonio Sanz, has said the region decided not to use the system that sends emergency alerts to mobile phones because it could not be tailored to specific communities.Officials have said some residents needed to evacuate while others were safer staying in their homes. They also argued an alert could have caused panic and traffic jams.The families reject that."Issue the damned alert!" said Chard. "Ring the bells, send the police guy out with his horn, go door to door, do everything."Thomas-Wolf Verdonckt, a Belgian virologist whose father Stanislas, 63, died, was on the phone to him as the flames approached.He says the victims "never received advice on what they should do, and certainly not warnings that they were in danger", and that the authorities' claim that everyone in the area was given adequate warning is not true."The only contact that the government managed to make with the victims was a couple of minutes before the flames engulfed everyone. One police car drove by with the sirens on. There was no talking, there was no messaging."Bédar's emergency plan was last approved in 2019, and regional officials say it was in the process of being updated. The municipality is classified by the Andalusian government as being at risk from wildfires.Of the 15 people who died in Bédar, 14 were foreign nationals: nine British citizens, three Belgian, one French and one American. The other victim was Spanish.In the days after the fire, Sanz faced a backlash for appearing to blame the victims. He said some people who made the decision to leave "at the last minute, took the wrong path".Verdonckt has been trying to find answers ever since the blaze."The morning afterwards, the Spanish officials brought out... a version of events which was simply the complete opposite of what I experienced," he said.He also believes a public inquiry is needed to prevent a similar disaster happening in Spain in the future."They are putting the safety of citizens in second place. That's simply not okay."'A huge hole in our lives'Danni Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, lost her parents Pete and Fran in the fire.They had lived in Bédar since 2018. Fran, a former headteacher, ran a quiz night that raised money for the local school and church."They were fantastic parents, my biggest champions and cheerleaders," said Danni. "They leave a huge, huge hole in our lives."She says her mother texted her at about 19:00 to say they had packed in case they had to leave."They were waiting for instructions, and those instructions didn't come," she said.Her parents died on the part of Bédar known as English Hill, one of the places where, families say, the authorities' only contact came minutes before the flames arrived.Gillam-Kirton says her grief has been made worse by the way the Spanish authorities have behaved since.Local police had told the family that Pete and Fran's car had been "meticulously searched" by forensic specialists and that she would find nothing.But in August, a month afterwards, Gillam-Kirton and her husband found what appeared to be human bones in the burnt-out car in which her father died. "I picked up what I recognised to be... part of a pelvis or a hip joint," she said.Gillam-Kirton fears they were her father's remains.Within minutes they also found her parents' mobile phones, jewellery, house keys and money. Police had earlier told the family that no personal belongings had survived.Spain's Guardia Civil police have been approached for comment.Image source, Danni Gillam-KirtonImage caption, Danni Gillam-Kirton says she found human bones and her parents' possessions in the burnt-out shell of their carThe fragments were eventually sent to Madrid for testing. The family says police have now told them no DNA was recovered and that the bones were those of an animal.But Gillam-Kirton says experts, including a forensic anthropologist who worked on the Grenfell Tower fire investigation, believe the fragments were human."We still don't know who or what they are," she said.Gillam-Kirton complained to the Guardia Civil. She says the reply told her only that the matter had been passed to the courts, and offered condolences for "the death of your relative", in the singular, when in fact she had lost both her parents."It feels like they're going to hope that we exhaust ourselves," she said. "Either the burden of grief is going to be enough for us to give up, or that we're going to financially exhaust ourselves."Gillam-Kirton says there is "a real lack of empathy when you're dealing with families that have lost so much".The one thing she wants above all is for someone to acknowledge what went wrong: "No-one seems to be willing to say 'do you know what, we made a mistake and for that we are sorry'."The death toll in Bédar was the highest from any single fire in Spain during the summer of 2026, and one of the largest in the country's history.Many victims were trapped as they tried to escape the village, as survivor Malcolm Timbrell told me outside his devastated home in July.The cause of the disaster, also known as the Los Gallardos fire after the neighbouring town where it started, is the subject of a criminal investigation.In July, the Guardia Civil said it was believed to have been started by a fallen power line, but that explanation has been called into question.The BBC has seen a letter in which the Andalusian government refused a request from Socialist MPs for its official reports on the fire. These included any documents explaining why no alert was sent to mobile phones.Image source, Gillam family handoutImage caption, Pete (far left) and Fran (far right) both died in the wildfire in July. Danni (second left) wants to know more about what happened to themThe letter, signed by Sanz in September, said the documents could not be released because the criminal investigation is under secreto de sumario, a court order keeping the case file confidential.Gillam-Kirton says the criminal case is focused on how the fire started, and that it will not necessarily examine the emergency response unless families pay lawyers to put that evidence before the judge."How can you have faith in these measures that they're putting in to mitigate future disasters if you don't know fully what happened the first time around?" she said."That's why you have a public inquiry," said Duncan Chard, "because the public need answers."Families in the UK, Belgium and Spain have set up various support groups, as well as a website called helpbedar.com.They have launched an appeal to pay for legal action, aiming to raise €100,000 (£83,000). Fundraising events are being held in both Spain and the UK, and so far about €11,000 has been collected.Relatives say their fight is like David and Goliath."We are getting steamrolled by the Andalusian government," said Chard.Ultimately, the families say all they want is answers, and for lessons to be learned so that others do not suffer the same ordeal.They say they want their fight to be a tribute to their loved ones who died."I feel like this is all I can do for them," said Gillam-Kirton.

schema.headline: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why

title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
description: Figure caption, BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the USByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentA US mid
body: Figure caption, BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the USByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondentA US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.What did the voter poll suggest?The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.This follows other recent Pew Research polling, external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered a "crucial or major factor" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).Did the AI backlash affect Senate races?But other factors would also have been motivating voters in these states, as elsewhere.BBC Verify analysis of state-level voter polling for Senate elections suggests states which swung to the Democrats either followed the national trend over data centre concerns, or seemed less concerned.So we can't say how many votes or Senate seats were directly delivered by data centre opposition.But it's notable that three key states in the US AI build-out, Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all elected Democrats as senators and governors who called for tighter regulation on data centres in one form or another.These proposals include:temporary bans on constructionending tax breaksrequirements to fully cover their own energy and water infrastructure costsmandates to use unionised construction workersstricter environmental and transparency safeguardslocal rights to vetoWhat could the election results mean for the future of the AI boom?The US economy has been heavily supported in recent years by massive corporate investments in AI, external, including for data centre construction.Official data, external shows inflation-adjusted monthly spending on building data centres, excluding the IT hardware to go into them, in August 2026 was $5bn (£4.2bn) - five times higher than in 2023.Analysis by Columbia Business School, external suggests AI infrastructure investment in the US is currently larger as a share of the overall economy than spending on new railways was at the height of that boom in the 19th Century.Cori Crider, executive director of the Future of Tech Institute, a European think tank, told BBC Verify the industry should anticipate that new state leaders will put conditions on or "even stop runaway data centre build".Seema Shah, from global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said requirements for developers to pay for additional investment in the electricity grid, meet tougher standards over their usage of resources like water, or give up tax incentives could "raise development costs and slow new supply".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Stargate Oracle AI data centre spans roughly four million square feet in Abilene, TexasHowever, Heather West from the Eurasia Group consultancy said temporary bans on construction and new regulations might delay the data centre roll out, but would not stop it entirely.She said "projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed", but delays would affect the "next wave" of building through "local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centres pay for their own power".Analysts from the consultancy Oxford Economics have said there are also strong economic incentives for politicians to avoid policies that would severely disrupt data centre construction, pointing to tax revenue and construction jobs they bring.Deepak Surana of the Futurum Group, a technology research firm, said he expected there would ultimately be "a negotiation, not a moratorium" from Texas state leaders on data centres to ensure no negative impact on residents' energy and water bills.OpenAI, which has a data centre in Texas and under-construction projects in Ohio, pledged to ensure it fully paid for its own electricity on Thursday, external - one day after the midterm results.Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett, Rob England and Christine JeavansGet in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?

schema.headline: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?

title: Major construction near Iran bases, satellite images suggest
description: ByShayan SardarizadehBenedict Garman and Matt MurphyBBC Verify  Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its m
body: ByShayan SardarizadehBenedict Garman and Matt MurphyBBC Verify  Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war. Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.At Karaj, external and Shahroud, satellite images appear to show significant excavation. At Karaj, multiple vehicles were visible in satellite images, while improvements appear to have been carried out to the nearby airbase.The images from Karaj appear to show "a new portal for an underground facility", said Sam Lair, research analyst at the Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), which has looked extensively into recent developments at Iranian sites. Analysis from Janes also indicates there appears to be a new facility under construction at Karaj, including tunnel entrances and structures which could indicate an expansion of nearby damaged or destroyed missile bases - or could also be for storage or other purposes.The construction work is unlikely to be part of an effort to deceive foreign intelligence agencies, said Janes analyst Sean O'Connor. He said such a project "would be costly and may achieve little".The developments come after repeated assurances from the White House that US-Israeli attacks have depleted the Iranian armed forces, which US President Donald Trump dismissed as a "complete and total mess".A Pentagon spokesperson previously said that the US had "destroyed up to 90% of Iran's drone, ballistic missile, and naval industrial base" and "significantly degraded" the country's ability to launch drone and missile attacks.But Iran claims it retains large stockpiles of missiles, and footage broadcast on state TV this week claimed to show dozens of missiles at the entrance to an underground facility in southern Iran. Back in August, state TV footage also claimed to show Khordad surface-to-air missiles emerging out of a tunnel near the southern city of Bandar Abbas, external.A MAIAR analyst also identified new construction and excavations outside tunnel entrances near the city of Qom, close to the Fordo underground uranium enrichment complex, which has been bombed by both the US and Israel multiple times.Activity related to military assets would show that Tehran is bracing itself for further attacks by the US and Israel, said Mark Cancian, a military analyst with International Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)."The purpose is to better defend itself against future attacks," he said. "It also indicates a priority on rebuilding military capability rather than rehabilitating the economy."Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler.

schema.headline: Major construction near Iran bases, satellite images suggest

title: Indonesia's presidential wiretapping scandal: What to know
description: Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversat
body: Authorities are investigating possible treason in Indonesia after a bombshell announcement this week that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations might have been spied on.Several senior figures of Prabowo's administration have been embroiled in the wiretapping scandal, including his chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - who is not related to the president despite his name.It is unfolding against what many have interpreted as a widening rift between Prabowo and his predecessor, Joko Widodo - otherwise know as Jokowi - who had thrown his support behind Prabowo's 2024 presidential campaign."Listyo's position, as we know, is actually very close to Jokowi," Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, told BBC Indonesian."So now it's practically said that they're going their separate ways."Listyo Sigit Prabowo, the president's chief of staff, was arrested on Tuesday along with two senior police officers for allegedly wiretapping President Prabowo.The three men are suspected of keying phone numbers, including Prabowo's, into the police's official electronic surveillance system - which allows authorities to intercept communications - without following proper procedures, such as obtaining an investigation warrant or case report.Authorities say the operation was discovered last week after a tip-off from a police officer. But they believe the alleged wiretapping stretches back to 2025, when Listyo was serving as the national police chief.This could amount to treason, as it involved "sensitive information" that could "endanger the interests and sovereignty of the nation", a spokesperson for the president told reporters on Wednesday.In Indonesia, treason is punishable by life imprisonment or even the death penalty - though the country has not executed anyone in a decade.The spokesperson said the motive behind the alleged wiretapping remained unclear.It was not just President Prabowo who was targeted in the alleged wiretapping operation, either. Other targets included politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople, authorities said.On Thursday evening, police named a fourth suspect: Slamet Uliandi, from the national police criminal investigation unit. But he was not detained due to his ill health after suffering a stroke, according to authorities.Listyo, who was appointed the president's chief of staff last month, was sacked from his new position shortly after his arrest.This is not the first wiretapping scandal to have involved Indonesia's leaders. In 2014, several wiretapping devices were discovered at Jokowi's official residence when he was the governor of Jakarta. Former president Megawati Soekarnoputri claimed in 2024 that she had avoided using her personal mobile phone number because she was the target of wiretapping. Indonesia's police chief Suyudi Ario Seto told reporters on Thursday that the probe into wiretapping was "purely law enforcement and has nothing to do with rivalries or anything else".But many see it as the latest blow in a disintegrating alliance between President Prabowo and former president Jokowi, who led the country from 2014 to 2024.Jokowi had thrown his support behind Prabowo in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, as part of an alliance that ultimately propelled Prabowo to become Indonesia's next leader.Riding to victory with him was Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Jokowi's eldest son, who became Indonesia's vice president.Two years on, that alliance appears to be fracturing - even if neither party has confirmed the rift.Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many of Jokowi's allies into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.Meanwhile, uncertainty also looms over Gibran, Jokowi's son, who is mired in a growing controversy over the validity of his high school credentials, a pre-requisite to run for vice presidency. He now faces calls to be disqualified from his job, on the grounds that he should not have been eligible as a candidate.The wiretapping scandal and subsequent arrest of Listyo - who rose to the top of the police force in Jokowi's administration, and is seen as one of the ex-president's longtime allies - is now adding to the tensions between Prabowo and Jokowi.When asked about the wiretapping incident after the court session on Thursday, Jokowi told reporters that "we should all respect the ongoing legal process".This latest scandal comes during a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. His flagship free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.Experts, meanwhile, say all this has distracted from the more pressing challenges that Indonesians are facing on the ground - from economic uncertainties to environmental pollution. In recent months, protesters have taken to the streets to pressure the government on a range of issues such as toxic wildfire haze, corruption, and cost-of-living woes."It's like we're living in a country on autopilot," Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia, told BBC Indonesian. "Because the way the government operates proves that it's not the people's interests that are being pursued, but rather the interests of individual groups."

schema.headline: Indonesia's presidential wiretapping scandal: What to know
